title: Furthest Building You Can Reach
description: Brute force to optimized: exploring every brick/ladder combination versus a size-capped min-heap that keeps ladders on the biggest climbs.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of building heights, and a number of bricks and ladders, start at building 0 and move to adjacent buildings. Moving from a shorter or equal building costs nothing; moving to a TALLER building requires either using (height difference) bricks, or using one whole ladder (regardless of the height difference). Return the furthest building index reachable.

blocks.text: Walk from building 0 as far right as possible, where climbing to a taller building costs either bricks equal to the height difference, or one ladder regardless of the difference, and both resources are limited.

blocks.title: Analogy: Rationing Climbing Gear for a Long Hike With Steep Sections
blocks.text: Picture a hike with a limited supply of energy bars (bricks, costing an amount proportional to how steep a climb is) and a limited number of climbing harnesses (ladders, each usable once regardless of how steep the climb is). Saving harnesses for the STEEPEST climbs, and paying with energy bars for the gentler ones, gets you the furthest overall.

blocks.caption: Save ladders for the biggest climbs; pay bricks for the smaller ones

blocks.text: Using the ladder on the biggest climb and bricks for the rest, the furthest reachable index is 4.
Before trying every combination of using a brick or a ladder at each climb, notice that ladders are most valuable on the BIGGEST climbs, since they save the most bricks there.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A ladder always costs exactly 1 "use," regardless of how big the climb is, while bricks cost exactly the climb size.

Observation 2: Using a ladder is most beneficial on the LARGEST climbs, since that avoids spending the most bricks.

Observation 3: Walking forward and tentatively assigning a ladder to every climb encountered, but capping the number of "active" ladder assignments at the available ladder count, and paying bricks for whichever assigned climb turns out to be the SMALLEST once that cap is exceeded, always keeps the ladders on the biggest climbs seen so far.

Observation 4: A min-heap of size "ladders" tracks exactly this: the smallest of the currently ladder-assigned climbs sits at the top, ready to be evicted (paid for with bricks) the moment a bigger climb needs a ladder instead.

This leads to walking forward, tentatively using a ladder for every climb, but maintaining only the "ladders" biggest climbs in that ladder-assigned set (via a min-heap), and paying bricks for whichever climb gets evicted.
At each climb, try both possible choices (use a brick, or use a ladder), exploring every combination recursively.

items: At each climb, if resources remain, try using a ladder and recursing, then try using bricks and recursing.
Track the furthest index reached across every combination of choices.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every climb triggers two recursive branches (ladder or bricks), whenever both are viable.
This explores exponentially many combinations, most of which are dominated by better choices.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential, exploring every combination of resource choices.
Space: O(n) for the recursion depth.

Limitation: most combinations are clearly suboptimal, using a ladder on a tiny climb while paying bricks for a huge one is never better than the reverse; a greedy rule removes the need to explore combinations at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why exploring every combination is wasteful: it is never beneficial to use a ladder on a SMALLER climb while paying bricks for a LARGER one; swapping the two assignments is always at least as good.

What the optimal assignment looks like: ladders should go to the "ladders" LARGEST climbs encountered so far, and bricks should cover everything else.

How to maintain this while walking forward: tentatively use a ladder for every climb, keeping a min-heap of the climbs currently "holding" a ladder; whenever the heap exceeds size "ladders," evict (pay bricks for) the smallest one, since it is the least valuable ladder use so far.

The core idea: walk forward, maintain a size-"ladders" min-heap of ladder-assigned climb sizes, and pay bricks immediately whenever a climb gets evicted; stop the moment bricks run out.

Walk through each climb. For every climb where the next building is taller, push the height difference onto a min-heap. If the heap now holds more than "ladders" climbs, pop the smallest one and pay for it with bricks; if bricks go negative, the previous building is the furthest reachable. Otherwise, continue to the end.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: min-heap capped at "ladders" size, pay bricks for the smallest evicted climb

blocks.text: Tentatively assigning a ladder to every climb, but immediately evicting (and paying bricks for) the smallest one whenever more than "ladders" are currently assigned, guarantees that at every point, the ladders are held by the largest climbs seen so far, exactly the optimal assignment. The walk stops the instant bricks cannot cover an evicted climb, since no better assignment of the given resources could have gone further.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log ladders), one heap operation per climb.
Space: O(ladders) for the heap.

blocks.text: Furthest Building You Can Reach is a greedy-plus-heap problem: ladders should always be reserved for the biggest climbs, and a size-capped min-heap maintains exactly that assignment while walking forward, without ever exploring alternate combinations.

items: Using a max-heap instead of a min-heap (the SMALLEST ladder-assigned climb is what should be evicted and paid for with bricks).
Forgetting that a climb where the next building is shorter or equal costs nothing at all.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how do you decide where to use a ladder versus bricks", think: ladders on the biggest climbs, tracked with a size-capped min-heap.

items: How would you determine which SPECIFIC climbs ended up using a ladder, not just the furthest index?
How would this change if ladders had varying costs, rather than all costing the same "1 use"?
Any "limited premium resource for the biggest values, cheaper resource for the rest" greedy-plus-heap problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in exponential time. The optimized size-capped min-heap approach runs in O(n log ladders) time and O(ladders) space.

items: Pattern: a greedy assignment (ladders to the biggest climbs) maintained with a size-capped min-heap.
Core Idea: tentatively use a ladder for every climb; whenever more than "ladders" are in use, pay bricks for the smallest one, since it is the least valuable ladder assignment.
Time: exponential for the brute force, O(n log ladders) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(ladders) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: ladders are always most valuable on the biggest climbs; a size-capped min-heap enforces this assignment automatically.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known greedy-plus-heap problem, quick once the eviction rule is recognized.
One line memory trick: min-heap capped at "ladders," evict (pay bricks for) the smallest climb on overflow.
